title: How to explain home inspection report to buyers on Mac, for realtors in 2026

description: Explain a home inspection report to buyers in plain words. Sort findings, quote costs with sources, and use free fixes on your Mac. Lazur can help.

intro: To explain a home inspection report to buyers, sort the findings into three groups: required, typically not required, and open to negotiation. Then cover the items that change price, safety, or timing, and say plainly which items you would not worry about. The steps below work with a PDF, a pen, and a clear follow-up email.
tldr: Sort every finding into three groups: required, typically not required, and open to negotiation. NAR uses those groups to describe repairs.
Lead with safety, structure, water, and price. Then cover the items you would not worry about, and say why.
Give a cost range only with its source. A camera scan was $175 in one Realtor's area, and a waste line replacement could run $15,000 to $20,000.
Explain what the inspection did not cover. A standard inspection does not fully cover septic systems, pests, radon, asbestos, water quality, or mold.
Send one written follow-up the same day. Check your brokerage's rules before any client report goes into an AI tool.

blocks.text: Most buyers read the inspection report alone, after a long day, with no one to ask. They open a long PDF, scroll past photos, and try to decide whether the house is fine. Your job is to turn that document into a short, honest talk. You can do it with a plain-language list, sourced costs, and a clear follow-up. None of it needs new software.
How to read a home inspection report: what it includes

A home inspection report lists what the inspector saw, tested, and judged. The ASHI Standard of Practice sets the minimum content. It requires the report to name systems that are not functioning properly, are significantly deficient, are unsafe, or are near the end of their service lives. It also requires a recommendation to correct or monitor each one. The standard does not require a summary page or a pass or fail grade.

ASHI approved a revised Standard in a member vote that closed January 8, 2026. The ASHI page does not give a start date. Ask the inspector which version the report follows, so you know what it was built to cover.

NAR notes that inspectors do not label homes pass or fail. It also warns that a dense, multipage report can cause anxiety. That anxiety is the first thing you manage. A buyer who sees many pages of findings may assume the house is a disaster. The same report, with a clear order, often feels smaller.
What the report can and cannot tell a buyer

A standard inspection is short and limited. Consumer Reports says it typically takes 2 to 4 hours, and inspectors usually finish the report within a day or two. Reports may include photos or video. The inspector can only point out problems they can see. A standard inspection does not fully cover septic systems, pests, radon, asbestos, water quality, or mold. Those need specialists.

blocks.text: Separate a finding from a limit. A finding is something the inspector saw. A limit is something the inspector did not check. A buyer who hears that the septic system was not inspected may think it passed. Say that it was outside the inspection, and say who should check it.

Also separate near end of life from broken. An older water heater that works is a planning item. A water heater that leaks is a repair item. The report may use similar wording for both. Say which is which, in one sentence each.
Sort findings into three groups before the call

NAR advises that a home inspection report is not a to-do list. It describes three groups of repairs. Some items the inspector considers required. Some are typically not required. Some are open to negotiation. Use those three groups as your labels. They give the buyer a sense of order and a shared vocabulary for the call.

items: Open the full report. Read every heading, even if a summary page exists.
Label each finding as required, typically not required, or open to negotiation. Ask the inspector to confirm your labels.
Mark anything that affects safety, the structure, or water. Put those items at the top of your list.
Write down each item the inspector could not inspect, and the reason given in the report.
Draft one plain sentence for each item the buyer is likely to ask about.

blocks.title: Ask for tags
blocks.text: Send the inspector a short email with the three labels and ask them to tag each item. You get a clearer list, and the buyer hears the labels from the person who wrote the report.
Walk through the big-ticket items with real numbers

Start the call with the items that change price, safety, or timing. Keep each one to a few sentences. For each one, say what the inspector saw, what they recommend, and who should check it next. Then give a cost range with its source. If you have no source, say you do not know and offer to find out.

Here is a worked example. Suppose the report notes slow drains and a sewer line of unknown condition. You say the inspector recommends a camera scan. Consumer Reports cites a camera scan at $175 in one Realtor's area. If the waste line must be replaced, the same article says the cost could be $15,000 to $20,000. The scan is the small step that tells the buyer which number applies.

Do not guess. A guessed figure is the fastest way to lose a buyer's trust. If the buyer asks what a roof replacement costs, say that the price depends on material, size, and region. Then offer to find local quotes and bring them back to the next call.
Explain the repairs you would not worry about

Telling a buyer what not to worry about is the part people skip. It is also the part that calms people down. Name the items that look like normal wear for the age of the home, the items the inspector tagged as typically not required, and the cosmetic items. Say why each one is low priority, in the inspector's words where possible.

Be careful with reassurance. You are not the inspector. Say the inspector marked an item as typically not required, and read them the note. Do not call an item fine unless the report says so. NAR's advice is to expect some imperfection and to treat it as normal. You can say the same thing, once the facts are on the table.
What to do when a buyer waives the home inspection contingency

Waivers are more common than they were. NAR members reported that 21% of buyers had waived the inspection contingency in September 2025. That was up from 17% in September 2024. According to NAR, a waiver shifts responsibility for repairs to the buyer. Your job is to make that trade-off clear, not to make the decision for them.

A 2025 Clever survey of 986 buyers found that 12% regret that the inspection missed problems. Another 8% regret that they cannot afford repairs. An inspection does not catch everything. Explain that before the buyer waives, and explain what an information-only inspection covers.

A home warranty may offset some of that risk, according to NAR, which cites a 2021 Washington Post article. Treat it as an option to research, not a fix. Read the coverage limits and exclusions before you suggest one.

blocks.title: Record the choice
blocks.text: Do not steer a buyer toward or away from an inspection. Describe the trade-off, let the buyer decide, and put the decision in a dated email.
Write the follow-up so the buyer can act on it

A call fades fast. Send a written follow-up the same day. Keep it short, in plain words, and in the same three groups you used on the call. Name the items, say what the inspector recommended, list the specialists to call, and state the next deadline. Do not add opinions the report does not support.

items: Top items in order, with the inspector's recommendation for each one.
Items typically not required, and why you are not worried about them.
Items open to negotiation, with any cost range and its source.
Specialists to call, such as a structural engineer for foundation cracks or a septic tester.
The next deadline from your contract, and who sends the next message.

blocks.text: Track each item in a sheet so nothing gets lost. In Google Sheets, make a column called Group. Select its cells, then go to Data > Data validation. Set the criteria to Dropdown and enter the three group names. Each row now takes one of three values. See [Google Sheets for realtors](/for/realtors/google-sheets) for the full setup.
Mistakes realtors make when explaining an inspection

items: Reading the summary aloud and skipping the sections that matter most.
Calling the house fine or bad before the buyer has read the report.
Giving a repair cost with no source and no range.
Treating a limit as a clean bill of health.
Answering structural, legal, or septic questions yourself instead of naming the right specialist.
Explaining on the phone with nothing in writing afterward.
Pasting a client's report into an AI tool before checking your brokerage's rules.

blocks.text: The last mistake is easy to make without noticing. Check your brokerage's rules before a client document goes into any tool, including AI tools. The rules come first, even when the tool seems harmless.
How Lazur helps you explain the report

Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac. It lives in the notch. Hold ⌥ ⌘ to ask about anything on screen, and Lazur answers out loud. If the report is open in Preview, ask what the roof section says in plain language. Ask where a finding is, and Lazur draws a circle and a label around it on your screen.

Lazur does not click buttons, open files, or edit documents for you. Ask it to guide you through a step, and it guides you one click at a time, waiting for each click. Lazur can also draft text for you to review. It does not send email for you.
Use dictation for the follow-up. Hold fn and speak. Lazur types clean, formatted text at the cursor in any app. Read the text before you send it, and fix any names or numbers that came out wrong.
Check your brokerage rules before you share a report

Inspection reports contain client information and property details. Before you share one with an AI tool, check your brokerage's rules. Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. When it answers, it sends the audio and the screenshot to AI providers. Lazur's privacy notes say that content is not stored and is never used to train AI models. Your brokerage's rules still come first.

If your brokerage has no written rule, ask your broker before you use any screen-reading tool with a client file. Reading a report on screen is one thing. Pasting client details into a shared chat is another.
Mac tools you already have for inspection reports

Preview handles most inspection PDFs on a Mac. Apple's Preview guide describes how to highlight, underline, and strike out text, and how to add notes and speech bubbles to a PDF. Open the report, then turn on the Markup toolbar from View > Show Markup Toolbar. Mark the items in each of your three groups with a different color, so the buyer can see the order.

Chrome keeps your sources in one place. Right-click a tab and choose Add tab to new group. Keep the NAR page, the ASHI standard, and the Consumer Reports article together. When a buyer asks a question, open the group and find the source quickly.

For the follow-up email, build the reply in Gmail. Save the closing paragraph you use every time as a template, so you do not retype it. See [Gmail for realtors on Mac](/for/realtors/gmail) for template setup and scheduled sends.
Start with the next report you receive

Pick the next inspection report on your desk. Read every heading, sort the items into three groups, and check every number against its source. Then make one call with the top items only. Send the written follow-up the same day. You do not need a new system to start.

faq.question: Should I explain every item in a home inspection report?
faq.answer: No. Start with items that affect safety, structure, water, or price. Then cover the items the inspector tagged as typically not required, in one short pass. NAR says a report is not a to-do list, so the buyer does not need to act on every line. Ask the buyer which systems matter most to them, and go deeper on those.

faq.question: Does a home inspection report give a pass or fail grade?
faq.answer: No. NAR says inspectors do not label homes pass or fail. The ASHI Standard of Practice requires the report to list deficient, unsafe, or end-of-life systems, with recommendations. It does not require a summary page. Tell the buyer this early, so they do not look for a grade that is not there.

faq.question: How much does a home inspection cost for a single-family home?
faq.answer: NAR, citing realtor.com, says an average home inspection for a single-family home generally runs $300 to $500. Home size, location, and scope change the price. A sewer camera scan costs extra. Consumer Reports cites $175 for one in one Realtor's area. Check local quotes before you quote a number to a buyer.

faq.question: What happens if a buyer waives the inspection?
faq.answer: NAR says waiving the inspection, or choosing an information-only inspection, shifts responsibility for repairs to the buyer. A home warranty may offset some of that risk. NAR members reported that 21% of buyers had waived the inspection contingency in September 2025. Put the buyer's choice and your explanation in a dated email.

faq.question: Can Lazur read an inspection report for me?
faq.answer: Lazur sees your screen only while you hold ⌥ ⌘. It answers out loud about what is visible, and it can point to a finding. It does not open, edit, or click through files for you. Read the report yourself, and use Lazur to clarify the parts you are unsure about.

faq.question: Is it safe to put a client's inspection report into an AI tool?
faq.answer: Check your brokerage's rules first. Those rules come before any tool. Lazur sends audio and a screenshot to AI providers to answer, and Lazur's privacy notes say those are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. If your brokerage restricts client data, do not share the report.

faq.question: Which Mac app opens an inspection report PDF?
faq.answer: Preview comes with macOS and opens PDFs. Apple's guide covers highlighting, underlining, striking out text, and adding notes and speech bubbles to a PDF. Turn on the Markup toolbar from View > Show Markup Toolbar. Your inspector may send a PDF you can open in any app.

faq.question: Who should answer questions about foundation cracks or septic systems?
faq.answer: Send those questions to the right specialist. Consumer Reports advises asking the inspector for referrals, such as a structural engineer for foundation cracks or a septic tester. A standard inspection does not fully cover septic systems. Do not diagnose the problem yourself.

costs.title: Income from deals that fall apart
costs.text: The May 2025 median pay for real estate sales agents was $52,830, and about 54% of sales agents are self-employed, according to BLS. A deal lost over a misunderstood report lands on your income directly. Your pay depends on closings, so a buyer who walks away at the wrong moment costs you more than a long call.

costs.title: Waivers that come back to you
costs.text: NAR members reported that 21% of buyers had waived the inspection contingency in September 2025, up from 17% a year earlier. A buyer who waives and later finds a problem may blame the agent. That blame can cost you referrals, even when the choice was theirs. Explain the trade-off before the buyer signs.

costs.title: Buyers who regret the inspection
costs.text: In a 2025 Clever survey of 986 buyers, 12% said they regret that the inspection missed problems. Another 8% regret that they cannot afford repairs. Those regrets are not all about the agent. Still, clear talk about scope helps the buyer avoid surprises later.

costs.title: Repeat calls and emails
costs.text: A rushed explanation can come back as more calls, more emails, and more questions. Those hours do not show up in a pay statement, but they take time from your next client. One written summary the same day can cut most of the repeat questions.

costs.title: Repair costs the buyer did not expect
costs.text: Consumer Reports says a waste line replacement could be $15,000 to $20,000. A camera scan was $175 in one Realtor's area. If the buyer did not expect a large number, they may feel you hid it. Give the range early, and give the source with it.

causes.title: The report is long and looks equally urgent
causes.text: Reports often list many items with the same layout and the same tone. NAR notes that a dense, multipage report can cause anxiety. A cracked tile and a leaking drain can look alike a few pages apart. The buyer does not know which item matters, so they assume all of them do. Your sort is the part they cannot do alone.

causes.title: There is no pass or fail grade
causes.text: NAR says inspectors do not label homes pass or fail. Buyers want a grade anyway. Without one, they make their own, and a long list of defects can feel like a fail. The ASHI standard does not require a summary page, so the summary is not guaranteed.

causes.title: The report arrives after the emotion
causes.text: A standard inspection takes 2 to 4 hours, and the report usually follows within a day or two. During that time the buyer has been hoping. Then they read the report alone, with no one to ask. The first reaction often happens before any question gets asked.

causes.title: Near end of life sounds like broken
causes.text: The ASHI standard requires inspectors to report systems near the end of their service lives. That is useful planning information. The words can still sound urgent to a buyer who has never owned a home. A working system flagged as near end of life can alarm a buyer who hears it for the first time.

causes.title: Limits look like clean bills of health
causes.text: The standard requires inspectors to list systems they did not inspect, with the reasons. Consumer Reports adds that a standard inspection does not fully cover septic systems, pests, radon, asbestos, water quality, or mold. Buyers may read a missing item as a passed item. That is a reading gap, not a lie, and it is easy to fix on the call.

causes.title: You are caught in the middle
causes.text: The buyer hears the inspector's words, then yours, and wonders whose side you are on. Agents may be tempted to soften a report, or to sound alarmed to seem protective. Either move creates a gap. Explain the report as written, then add your view and label it as your view.

fixes.title: Read the full report before the buyer does
fixes.text: Set aside focused time before the call. Read every heading, not only the summary. Mark each item as required, typically not required, or open to negotiation. NAR uses these groups to describe repairs, so the labels match what the buyer may hear elsewhere. Note any item you cannot explain yet, and ask the inspector.

fixes.title: Ask the inspector the right questions
fixes.text: Consumer Reports advises asking whether a problem would be a deal breaker for the inspector or for a family member. Also ask which items need a specialist, such as a structural engineer for foundation cracks or a septic tester. Ask the inspector to confirm which items they would tag as required.

fixes.title: Get the buyer to attend the inspection
fixes.text: NAR advises buyers to attend the inspection. At the property, the inspector can show plumbing and electrical components and explain the scope of a problem. Ask your buyer to attend and to bring a notepad. A buyer who sees the water heater understands a finding faster than one who only reads about it.

fixes.title: Explain scope before the number
fixes.text: Start with what the inspection covered and what it did not. Then give the finding. Then give the cost range, with its source. The order matters. A cost with no scope sounds like a verdict, and a finding with scope sounds like information.

fixes.title: Use the same labels every time
fixes.text: Pick plain labels and reuse them. Required, typically not required, and open to negotiation work well. Use the same words on the call, in the sheet, and in the email. Consistent labels help the buyer see what changed between the call and the follow-up.

fixes.title: Give a range only with a named source
fixes.text: Quote a cost range only when you have a source. Consumer Reports gives a $175 camera scan and a $15,000 to $20,000 replacement range, both from specific areas and a specific case. Say that these are examples, not averages. Check your own market before you quote a number.

fixes.title: Track every item in one sheet
fixes.text: Use a Google Sheet with one row per item. Add columns for the item, the group, the inspector's note, the source for any cost, the status, and the next step. Use Data > Data validation for the group column. The buyer's questions then stay in one place, and you can answer them from the same file.

fixes.title: Name the next step, not only the problem
fixes.text: Buyers need a next step, not only a list. In plain words, explain the options the contract allows, such as asking for a repair, asking for a credit, or accepting the item as it is. Confirm the deadline in the contract with your broker before you describe it to the buyer.

fixes.title: Keep a written question log
fixes.text: Write down every question the buyer asks, with the date. Answer each one in writing the same day when you can. Save your best answers as Gmail templates for the next buyer, after you check your brokerage's rules on client data.

plan.label: Day 0
plan.title: Before the inspection
plan.text: Ask the buyer to attend the inspection. Confirm with the inspector what is in scope and what is not. Tell the buyer the report sorts items into groups, so they know to listen for the labels.

plan.label: Day 1
plan.title: When the report arrives
plan.text: Read every heading. Sort each item into required, typically not required, or open to negotiation. Check every cost figure against a named source before you quote it.

plan.label: Day 2
plan.title: The walk-through call
plan.text: Cover the top items only. Lead with scope, then the finding, then the cost range. Ask the buyer what they want to focus on, and note the questions you cannot answer yet.

plan.label: Day 3
plan.title: Written follow-up
plan.text: Send the summary the same day as the call. Include the specialists to call and the next deadline from the contract. Keep a copy in your sent folder.

plan.label: Day 4
plan.title: Open questions
plan.text: Check whether the buyer has booked specialists. Answer open questions in writing. Log the buyer's decision, whatever it is, with the date.
